doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Bass playing, avant-garde and the state of the music
title: Richard Davis practicing and today's schooled bassists
summary: Ware contrasts Richard Davis's hours of practice with his own, and the schools available to young players.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: But Richard Davis says that he practices -- or Ron Carter, for instance, says that he practices an awful lot.
Yeah, well, those kind of cats do. I remember Richard in Chicago, way before he left, I first met him. He invited me over to his house and he had the books be-

fore him and he was up in his room, big beautiful collie dog. Richard would get up there and he'd practice six, seven hours. That was the applied -- I guess that's what his teachers told him he'd have to do in order to master his instrument. But see --
How do people reconcile the concept? Because playing -- classically trained bassists and, for lack of a better term -- a jazz bassist, they're two different approaches to the instrument.

Well, that's true. But if you notice now, most of the musicians coming out, they're more technical because they got schools for it. They're learning it, see, and before, when I was coming along, you might drop out of school because you had to earn some money just to live. Now the kids can go, go to high school -- it's there if they want to go. You know, they can -- they got teachers to teach them certain things and if you see someone with some talent, might give him a scholarship, you know? So long as his family's working or earning a living, they can keep going to school. You don't have to drop out to help the family live, you know.

Like I did, I dropped out because I needed clothes to wear, you know? So, I learned a different way. But all the kids coming up now, they know the books.
